1.pericope_label: At the same time, saith the Lord, will I be the God of all the families of Israel, and they shall be my people. Thus saith the Lord, The people which were left of the sword found grace in the wilderness; even Israel, when I went to cause him to rest.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch have the prophet speaking in the name of the people and counting himself one of them; while Israel languished in exile the Lord had withdrawn and kept himself at a distance, and the distance from which he now appears is Zion, where he is enthroned and from which he sits to lead them home. They give the closing verb its force as prolonging favour, so that because the love is everlasting grace has been kept up and the people not destroyed. Ellicott makes the union of the ten tribes with the two the thing filling the prophet's mind, since he cannot bear that a cleavage running through the religious and social life of the people should be made permanent, and calls this the crown of the promise closing the previous chapter; on the survivors of the sword he holds both ends at once, the captives who had escaped or would escape the Chaldeans and find grace in the desert between Palestine and the Euphrates, and the more distant exiles beyond the Tigris, giving as his reason that the older deliverance involved no such escape from a sword, which is why the language here is modified; he also treats a past experience of love as offered for the pledge of a future one, and reads the clause about causing Israel to rest as taking in settling and establishing, with the verb imperative in form.

Gill reads the time-marker forward to the days of the Gospel, when the Jews will weigh the old prophecies against what has happened and turn; on the survivors he looks back to the exodus, naming the sword of Pharaoh at the sea, the Amalekites and Amorites, and their own brethren after the calf and the affair at Baalpeor. Calvin reports that interpreters agree in taking the infinitive of the resting clause as a past tense, notes that some refer it to God as the leader who brings his people to rest, prefers the simpler sense of Israel betaking himself to his own rest, offers a version of his own, and remarks how widely the early translations diverge at this point.

Clarke stands back from the chapter and describes it as a piece of staging: a distant scene opens with God expressing his regard and promising restoration; heralds appear on Mount Ephraim proclaiming the arrival of the great jubilee and summoning the people to Zion; God resumes with promises so gracious that the nations are called to attend; and then, by what Clarke calls a very happy invention, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin is raised from her tomb near Jerusalem to look for her children and lament that none are in the land, before Ephraim comes into view to bewail his own past errors. On the survivors he takes them for the ten tribes who escaped the Assyrians, with the land of exile as the wilderness.

Henry works the word families hard: not the two tribes only but all of them, not the house of Aaron and the families of Levi only but every family, and not the state at large only but particular households, from which he draws the note that the families of good people may apply to God in their family capacity and stay themselves on him. On the survivors he makes the whole verse a reminder of what God did for the fathers coming out of Egypt.

debates.question: Whose sword had the survivors escaped?

positions.position: Pharaoh's at the sea, and the swords of Amalek, the Amorites and their own brethren after the calf; the exodus generation is meant.
The Assyrians', the ten tribes being the escapers and the land of exile the wilderness.
The Chaldeans', and also the earlier exile beyond the Tigris; the older deliverance had no such escape from a sword, which is why the language is modified here.

debates.question: What is meant by causing Israel to rest?

positions.position: Settling or establishing as well as giving rest, the verb being imperative in form: let me go to set him at rest.
Israel betaking himself to his own rest; the referring of it to God as leader is reported but not preferred.
The Lord leading his people through the wilderness to the sacred height, the distance being Zion where he is enthroned.

outliers.claim: Reads the whole chapter as staged drama, with heralds entering to proclaim a jubilee and a dead matriarch raised from her tomb to search for her children, a device he calls a very happy invention.
Turns the phrase about all the families of Israel into a domestic doctrine, that households may apply to God in their family capacity and stay themselves upon him as their God.

themes: At the same time, saith the Lord, will I be the God of all the families of Israel, and they shall be my people.
Thus saith the Lord, The people which were left of the sword found grace in the wilderness; even Israel, when I went to cause him to rest.

3.pericope_label: The Lord hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee. Again I will build thee, and thou shalt be built, O virgin of Israel: thou shalt again be adorned with thy tabrets, and shalt go forth in the dances of them that make merry. Thou shalt yet plant vines upon the mountains of Samaria: the planters shall plant, and shall eat them as common things. For there shall be a day, that the watchmen upon the mount Ephraim shall cry, Arise ye, and let us go up to Zion unto the Lord our God.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the rebuilding for a permanent condition of increasing prosperity, the repeated verb confirming the promise, the virgin being the congregation entering a new and joyful phase; on the vines they add the contrast with planting for strangers who destroy the fruit; and on the watchmen they make them men posted on the hills to catch the first crescent after the new moon, so the festivals could be fixed. Ellicott changes the axis of the opening clause, since the Hebrew adverb points to distance rather than time, so that a deliverer hears his people's cry from far off and draws near; he lists the competing versions of the drawing, that God has respited them or continued his lovingkindness, and sides with the older translations; says the building is more than towers and masonry and makes the instrument a drum of the tambourine kind with bells on its hoop; and on the watchmen he calls what follows all but decisive for the new-moon reading, the point being that the rival worship which had kept the ten tribes from the Temple was to cease.

Gill canvasses three owners for the words about an appearance long ago: the prophet, the eternal Son, or the church acknowledging past mercies while complaining they are old and that God now hides his face; he notes the word saying is not in the text, which is what wrongly turns the sequel into more of her speech. He turns the virgin into the church, espoused as a chaste virgin and built of living stones, and reads the planting of Gospel churches in the vines. Calvin hears in the opening clause a clamour raised by unbelievers wanting a pretext for rejecting favour, and says that is how profane men still deride whatever God has testified in Law, Prophets or Gospel; he rejects the common rendering of the drawing as frigid and unsuitable, reading a mercy that follows the people from year to year in every age; he uses the delay itself, since seventy years might have extinguished faith when nothing appears but the bare word and God repeats the same promise daily, so that we measure his power by our own and conclude that one who comes late will never come; on the vines he sets the promise against the old curse that another shall eat what you plant; and on the watchmen he observes the prophet deliberately includes the ten tribes.

Clarke collects three renderings of the everlasting love, with the old love, with a love of long standing, and simply I love thee always, taking it of the love shown the fathers in Egypt, the desert and the land, and then argues against making the verse a decree of election, since few Jews since the return from Babylon have given evidence of being God's children, the words concerning their state as a people preserved by providence as a proof of the authority of the Scriptures. He sees a veiling in the cloud, the women of the east wearing costly veils, explains the title virgin as marking a restoration to ancient purity, and takes the watchmen simply for the prophets calling both kingdoms to one worship. Wesley notes mountains suit vines, being open to the sun, and finds the fulfilment of the watchmen's cry where the gospel was received in Galilee and Samaria.

debates.question: Who speaks the words about an appearance long ago?

positions.position: Most likely the church, acknowledging past mercies and complaining they are old; the prophet and the eternal Son are canvassed too.
Unbelievers, raising a blasphemous clamour to excuse themselves for rejecting favour.
Nobody in particular; the adverb is spatial, not temporal, and the sense is that God appears from afar.

debates.question: Who are the watchmen on Mount Ephraim?

positions.position: Men posted on the hills to catch the first crescent after the new moon, so that the feasts could be fixed.
The prophets, calling both kingdoms to a single worship.

outliers.claim: Argues the verse cannot be about a decree of election toward the Jews, on the ground that few since the return from Babylon have given evidence of being God's children, and refers it instead to their preservation as a people.

Explains why a delay of seventy years is fatal to faith: when nothing appears but the bare word and the same promise is repeated daily, men measure God's power by their own and conclude that one who comes late will never come.

themes: The Lord hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.
Again I will build thee, and thou shalt be built, O virgin of Israel: thou shalt again be adorned with thy tabrets, and shalt go forth in the dances of them that make merry.
Thou shalt yet plant vines upon the mountains of Samaria: the planters shall plant, and shall eat them as common things.
For there shall be a day, that the watchmen upon the mount Ephraim shall cry, Arise ye, and let us go up to Zion unto the Lord our God.

7.pericope_label: For thus saith the Lord; Sing with gladness for Jacob, and shout among the chief of the nations: publish ye, praise ye, and say, O Lord, save thy people, the remnant of Israel. Behold, I will bring them from the north country, and gather them from the coasts of the earth, and with them the blind and the lame, the woman with child and her that travaileth with child together: a great company shall return thither. They shall come with weeping, and with supplications will I lead them: I will cause them to walk by the rivers of waters in a straight way, wherein they shall not stumble: for I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch supply a reason for telling the remotest heathen at all, lest they imagine the God of Israel wanted power to save his own and that they might learn to fear him. Ellicott renders the second phrase over the head of the nations, meaning over Israel, a title another prophet suggests the ten tribes claimed, and has even the heathen called to rejoice in the restoration and pray for its prosperity, the verb for saving being the one that became the cry of Hosanna; he makes the phrase about the ends of the earth wide enough for both Judah in Babylon and Israel in the cities of the Medes; he notices that precisely those usually left behind as encumbrances are named, the blind, the lame, the woman with child and the woman in labour, and concludes that none is to remain behind; on the weeping he will have all three at once, sorrow for the past, joy for the present and prayer for the future, with a partial fulfilment at the laying of the second foundation where the old men wept while the rest shouted; and he hears in the word firstborn an echo of what was said to Pharaoh, marking Ephraim for special favour now the birthright had passed from Reuben.

Gill takes the summons to sing for the Gentile Christians called to rejoice over the conversion of the Jews, which will be to them as life from the dead, but reports a Jewish reading which shifts the words and makes it the Lord saying to Jacob, sing with gladness, as the old versions and the Targum do; he takes the north of Babylon at the seventy years' end and then of the northern countries where the Jews are now numerous; and on the weeping he offers both tears of joy, on two Jewish commentators' authority, and tears of repentance for their sins and above all for rejecting the Messiah. Calvin fixes the moment of utterance, since the prophecy was given when the destruction of people, city and temple was close at hand, so the prophet was comforting the dead in their graves, to make them wait patiently and be sure that raising the dead is no harder for God than healing the sick; he observes that whenever the prophets speak of deliverance they name the north, as when they threaten they say the army comes from the north, the earlier deliverance having come from the south because Egypt lay there; and he rejects the joy reading of the weeping, taking the verse adversatively, that they went into exile weeping and that is no impediment to their restoration, on the model of the psalm of the sower, pressed hard, since exile was a sowing and the seed must die in the ground or stay barren.

Clarke agrees the chief of the nations is Jacob, this people having once been the most honourable on earth, and leaves the prayer open between the Jews interceding for their brethren and praising God for saving the remnant; he divides the exiles, the ten tribes having been carried partly into Assyria and partly into Media, countries far enough off to be called in prophetic language the coasts of the earth; he makes the return a promise of provision, difficulties removed and the journey supplied so that the veriest invalids arrive; takes the weeping as penitential only, men deeply deploring their sins while begging for mercy; and says Ephraim, the most considerable tribe, commonly stands for the whole ten. Wesley thinks the tense of the weeping may be past rather than future, so that they went weeping, citing the same psalm as Calvin, though allowing a weeping for joy as well as sorrow, and reads the rivers of water against the older journey out of Egypt, through a wilderness where water often failed.

debates.question: Is the weeping of the returning exiles grief or gladness?

positions.position: Either; tears of joy on Jewish authority, or tears of repentance for their sins and for rejecting the Messiah.
Penitential only, men deploring their sins while begging mercy.
All three together: sorrow for the past, joy for the present, prayer for the future.
Grief, and the clause is adversative: they went into exile weeping, and that is no impediment to their return.

debates.question: Who is called to sing for Jacob?

positions.position: The Gentile Christians, over the conversion of the Jews; though a Jewish reading, followed by the old versions, makes it addressed to Jacob himself.
The heathen, called to rejoice in Israel's restoration and pray for its prosperity.
Either the Jews interceding for their brethren or the Jews praising God for saving the remnant.

outliers.claim: Dates the oracle to the eve of the destruction and describes the prophet as comforting the dead in their graves, since a people about to be buried had to be made sure that raising the dead is no harder for God than healing the sick.
Reads the naming of the blind, the lame and the woman in labour as deliberate, since those are exactly the people an expedition leaves behind, and the point is that none shall be left.

themes: For thus saith the Lord; Sing with gladness for Jacob, and shout among the chief of the nations: publish ye, praise ye, and say, O Lord, save thy people, the remnant of Israel.

Behold, I will bring them from the north country, and gather them from the coasts of the earth, and with them the blind and the lame, the woman with child and her that travaileth with child together: a great company shall return thither.

They shall come with weeping, and with supplications will I lead them: I will cause them to walk by the rivers of waters in a straight way, wherein they shall not stumble: for I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.

10.pericope_label: Hear the word of the Lord, O ye nations, and declare it in the isles afar off, and say, He that scattered Israel will gather him, and keep him, as a shepherd doth his flock. For the Lord hath redeemed Jacob, and ransomed him from the hand of him that was stronger than he. Therefore they shall come and sing in the height of Zion, and shall flow together to the goodness of the Lord, for wheat, and for wine, and for oil, and for the young of the flock and of the herd: and their soul shall be as a watered garden; and they shall not sorrow any more at all. Then shall the virgin rejoice in the dance, both young men and old together: for I will turn their mourning into joy, and will comfort them, and make them rejoice from their sorrow. And I will satiate the soul of the priests with fatness, and my people shall be satisfied with my goodness, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch keep to the picture of the redeemed streaming out from the sacred height and spreading over the country like water for the good things dealt out at home, observe that the dancing belongs only to the virgins, the young men and old sharing the joy but not the figure, and take the fatness for the fat of the thank-offerings, restored worship bringing the priests their share again. Ellicott makes the isles a vague representative of the distant west, and takes both nations and isles for heathen invited into Israel's praise; on the two verbs for deliverance he distinguishes setting free from acting as the near kinsman, who was liberator and avenger both, and denies that the notion of a price paid lies in the Hebrew.

Gill widens the beneficiary of the redemption from the patriarch and his natural posterity to all the elect of whatever nation, and rejects the maintenance of ministers as too low a sense for the priests' fatness, offering either their being filled with the doctrine they must feed others with or, the gospel knowing no separate order of priests, the whole body of the saints. Calvin explains the lofty strain, since seventy years is a whole lifetime, the people had been buried as in a grave, and the length of time alone was enough to cut off hope, so the prophet exclaims and despatches heralds everywhere; he supplies the objection answered, that the Chaldean monarchy looked like a gulf that had swallowed the world so that men comparing their case with any imaginable remedy would despair, though sheep in the jaws of wolves are not beyond rescue; he makes the height of Zion the point of the whole return, since the promise is of the Temple restored, without which the journey home mattered little, for if only quietness, wealth and pleasure were in question they had better have stayed in a fertile and agreeable Chaldea, and what made returning worth doing was separation from the heathen and the right worship of God; he admits Israel danced while celebrating God's praises but insists it was chaste and a mode of worship, nothing like the wantonness the world indulges in when happy; and he explains why the priests are singled out, as the heart of the people, the nation being incomplete without a priesthood, since without it they would have lived like heathen with no prescribed way of calling on God.

Clarke fills the watered garden with the light, life and power of God, so that they rejoice evermore and give thanks in everything, makes the flowing together the gathering at the yearly feasts, and agrees the fatness is the fat of the thank-offerings restored to the priests with the worship. Wesley identifies the height of Zion with the Temple, reads the deliverance and the entry into the land as types, of redemption by Christ and of the saints entering heaven, and takes soul here for the whole man, reading the gospel's joy and heaven's under the same words.

Henry treats the summons as news, since this is a work the nations cannot help noticing, so let them hear the prophecy in order to understand the performance and pass it to the isles; it will spread the world over and look great in history, and we may see first how it looks in prophecy. He compresses the promise into an epigram, that the hand which gave the wound shall heal it, since he who scattered knows where and therefore where to find them; he reaches the same conclusion as Ellicott by another route, that the redemption is by power and not by price, as of old out of Egypt; he recalls the singing when the foundation was laid; and he says our souls are never worth calling gardens except as watered by the dews of the Spirit, adding that the promise about sorrow has no full accomplishment this side of the heavenly Zion.

debates.question: Does the redemption involve a price?

positions.position: No; the second verb is the near kinsman's act of liberating and avenging, and the notion of a price paid is not in the Hebrew.
No; it is by power and not by price, as of old out of Egypt.
The point is the certainty rather than the mechanism, the deliverance being a type of the redemption by Christ.

debates.question: Who are the priests to be satiated with fatness?

positions.position: The literal priests, receiving their share of the thank-offerings again as worship is restored.
Either gospel ministers filled with the doctrine they must feed others with, or the whole body of the saints, since the gospel knows no separate order of priests.
The literal priests, singled out because the priesthood was the heart of the people and the nation would be incomplete without it.

outliers.claim: Argues that for merely earthly goods the exiles had better have stayed in Chaldea, which was fertile and agreeable, and that what made the return worth making was separation from the heathen and the restored worship of God.
Reduces the promise to an epigram, that the hand which gave the wound shall heal it, since the one who scattered them knows where he scattered them and therefore where to find them.

themes: Hear the word of the Lord, O ye nations, and declare it in the isles afar off, and say, He that scattered Israel will gather him, and keep him, as a shepherd doth his flock.
For the Lord hath redeemed Jacob, and ransomed him from the hand of him that was stronger than he.

Therefore they shall come and sing in the height of Zion, and shall flow together to the goodness of the Lord, for wheat, and for wine, and for oil, and for the young of the flock and of the herd: and their soul shall be as a watered garden; and they shall not sorrow any more at all.
Then shall the virgin rejoice in the dance, both young men and old together: for I will turn their mourning into joy, and will comfort them, and make them rejoice from their sorrow.
And I will satiate the soul of the priests with fatness, and my people shall be satisfied with my goodness, saith the Lord.

15.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not. Thus saith the Lord; Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the Lord; and they shall come again from the land of the enemy. And there is hope in thine end, saith the Lord, that thy children shall come again to their own border.

schools.summary: Ellicott presses the name Ramah: the noun carries the article elsewhere when it is a proper name and here stands without one, so the sense may be simply from a mountain height, as the Latin version took it, and if a place is meant it is probably the one in Benjamin. He adds the structural point, that the contrast with the exulting joy just before shows a new section beginning, repeating in altered form the same pair of pictures, present woe and future gladness, with Rachel as mother of Joseph standing for the northern kingdom; he works at what the work is, tracing the phrase to an older prophecy delivered to a king of Judah and reading Rachel as labouring at repentance and reformation with a mother's care, comforted that the labour will not be wasted, while setting aside the alternative that refers the work to the travail of childbirth; and he improves the last clause to hope for thy future, defining the hope as the return of the ten tribes. Keil and Delitzsch keep the promise in the same terms, a reward for the work and a return from the enemy's land.

Gill notes the word means a high place, which is why the Targum paraphrases rather than transliterates; he allows sorrow of this kind may lawfully be indulged but holds it must be moderated, and that when relief comes from God himself the mournful voice is to stop and wet eyes to be dried; and on the last clause he takes the posterity sense and pushes it to the children who had been massacred rising again to a blessed immortality. Calvin is more interested in the device than the geography, since this is a personification, a woman long dead and reduced to ashes raised up to lament, and the discourse has more force that way than if the prophet had said the land would look waste and mournful; he notes the rhetoricians rank personification among the highest ornaments and that a Roman authority on style held nothing moves an audience so much as raising the dead from below, the prophet adorning his speech in that very manner though never taught in their schools. He insists the point is not that grief is forbidden but that it will not be perpetual, since the exiles will return and the land that fell to Benjamin and Joseph will be inhabited again; and he uses the word end to establish the shape of the oracle, since had their happiness run in one unbroken stream the word would not suit, a contrast being intended between the end and the beginning.

Clarke fixes Ramah as the town six or seven miles from Jerusalem, near which Rachel was buried, and says the evangelist, ever fond of accommodation, applied the words because they suited the occasion, stating plainly they are not a prediction of that event; at the next verse he presses it, since those murdered infants never came again from the land of the enemy, whereas the exiles did. Wesley makes Ramah the place where the Babylonian captain sorted the prisoners, releasing some, condemning others, sending the rest away, which caused the bitter weeping, and simply records that there was a lamentation like this one when the infants around Bethlehem were killed.

debates.question: Is Ramah a place or a height?

positions.position: Possibly not a place at all; the noun lacks the article it carries elsewhere as a proper name, so the sense may be from a mountain height.
The town in Benjamin, six or seven miles from Jerusalem, near Rachel's burial.
The place where the Babylonian captain disposed of the prisoners.
The word means a high place, which is why the Targum paraphrases it.

debates.question: Does the passage predict the killing of the children at Bethlehem?

positions.position: No; the evangelist applied words that suited the occasion, and the promise of a return from the enemy's land could never be said of murdered infants.
There was a lamentation like this one then, and the two stand side by side without further adjudication.

outliers.claim: Defends the raising of a dead woman to lament as a rhetorical device, noting that the rhetoricians rank personification among the highest ornaments and that a Roman authority held nothing moves an audience so much as raising the dead.
Extends the hope for the latter end to the massacred children themselves, who are to rise again and enjoy a blessed immortality.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not.
Thus saith the Lord; Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the Lord; and they shall come again from the land of the enemy.
And there is hope in thine end, saith the Lord, that thy children shall come again to their own border.

18.pericope_label: I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself thus; Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised, as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke: turn thou me, and I shall be turned; for thou art the Lord my God. Surely after that I was turned, I repented; and after that I was instructed, I smote upon my thigh: I was ashamed, yea, even confounded, because I did bear the reproach of my youth.

schools.summary: Ellicott keeps the northern exiles in view, longest under the discipline of suffering, so they must by now have learnt repentance, and in it, treated as accomplished, the prophet finds fresh ground of hope for Judah; he calls the bullock comparison the nearest thing in the older Scriptures to the Greek proverb about kicking against the goads; he reports a commentator who refers the turning back to the apostasy rather than forward to repentance and rejects it, the word repeating the one used a verse before and being more naturally a penitent's first motion; and he ranges the smiting of the thigh with the publican's smiting on his breast as an Eastern expression of extremest grief, quoting Homer for the gesture.

Gill takes the name Ephraim for Israel, the ten tribes and even the whole nation, reads the passage of their conversion in a later day, and grants the patriarch himself, a tender-hearted man, could be introduced as Rachel just was; on the order of the experiences he puts conversion first and repentance after, since the prayer was answered and only then came repentance, not of gross actions only but of inward corruptions and even of sins in holy things, which is evangelical repentance and cannot precede a real turning. Calvin puts it doctrinally, that a sinner's repenting is God's peculiar work and cannot be ascribed to human strength, and closes on the use of the whole: we shun whatever is hard to the flesh, so we must regard the end, and when we see God had our salvation in view while handling us roughly the sorrow is lessened, since had he indulged them their pride would only have grown.

Clarke has the speaker confess he was an unbroken and untoward steer who rebelled the more he was chastised and has profited only now, and a man willing at last to take the yoke and finding he has no power, able only to will and pray, so he asks God to take the matter into his own hand; he orders the experiences differently from Gill, making conviction first, since as soon as a man sees himself lost he is convicted and contrition follows conviction; and he says smiting the thigh was a usual sign of deep affliction and the same among the ancient Greeks, quoting two passages of Homer with an English poet's rendering and adding he has often seen people in deep grief do it. Wesley notes such beasts are unruly when first yoked and makes the reproach of youth the just punishment of sins long committed.

Henry says the singular marks unanimity, so they should be as one man in repenting, and also fits the words to particular penitents, recalling the man of that name mourning for his children many days; he allows two senses to the admission of being chastised, either that it was well he was, since otherwise he had been undone, or that it records a want of feeling, the chastisement being all there was; he hears in the prayer a man bent to backslide who cannot keep close to God, still less bring himself back, so that unless grace turns him he will wander endlessly, though God works with power and makes the unwilling willing; he keeps the gesture moral rather than antiquarian, the man amazed at his own stupidity and unable to look up to God with confidence; and he observes that finding one sin should set us searching for more, the sin of our youth being its reproach and to be remembered against ourselves in penitential shame.

debates.question: Which comes first, the turning or the repenting?

positions.position: Conversion first and repentance after, since evangelical repentance cannot precede a real turning.
Conviction first, since a man who sees himself lost is convicted, and contrition follows conviction.
The turning is the first motion of a penitent, not a reference back to the earlier apostasy.

debates.question: What does the admission of having been chastised confess?

positions.position: Either that the chastisement was necessary, or that it was felt and no more, nothing being awakened by it.
That he rebelled the more he was chastised and has profited only now.
That the punishment was not without fruit, since God had the sinner's salvation in view while handling him roughly.

outliers.claim: Leaves the text for the classics on the smiting of the thigh, quoting two passages of Homer in the original with an English poet's version, and adding that he has often seen people in deep grief do the same.
Turns the whole passage into an argument about the use of affliction: since we shun whatever is hard to the flesh, we must look to the end, and indulgence would only have grown their pride.

themes: I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself thus; Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised, as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke: turn thou me, and I shall be turned; for thou art the Lord my God.
Surely after that I was turned, I repented; and after that I was instructed, I smote upon my thigh: I was ashamed, yea, even confounded, because I did bear the reproach of my youth.

20.pericope_label: Is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child? for since I spake against him, I do earnestly remember him still: therefore my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him, saith the Lord. Set thee up waymarks, make thee high heaps: set thine heart toward the highway, even the way which thou wentest: turn again, O virgin of Israel, turn again to these thy cities. How long wilt thou go about, O thou backsliding daughter? for the Lord hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man.

schools.summary: Ellicott sets out both readings of the opening question: affirmatively the words are a father's yearning over a son still loved, God wondering at his own affection for so rebellious a creature; negatively they press the faults as destroying all claim to love. He judges the affirmative far the better, since every word of reproof or invitation here carries a loving remembrance. On the next clause he corrects the version, the preposition hardly meaning against, for which this prophet uses other words, the sense being rather as often as I speak to him. He notices the figure changing, from Ephraim the dear son to Israel the backsliding daughter, and has the first returning party set the waymarks up for those who follow, so the road walked in shame is walked again in joy; he makes the reproach that follows the pacing to and fro of impatient desire, the penitent but still adulterous wife hesitating between her lovers and her husband; and on the last clause he fixes the translators' sense by a line of Shakespeare, where to compass is to woo and win, finding the point in an inversion, since the bridegroom woos but here the erring wife shall woo her divine husband. He lists and dismisses the alternatives, that a woman shall be turned into a man, or protect one, or put one to flight, and says the connection with the Incarnation belongs to dreams rather than realities, lacking even an allusion in the New Testament and excluded by the word used for woman.

Gill grants a question in this Hebrew form usually denies the more vehemently, which would make Ephraim no dear son, but says that runs against the scope of the passage and renders it is not Ephraim my dear son, to which the answer is yes; he takes the reproach geographically, of wandering from country to country as the Jews still do, and notes the word carries the sense of folly in Arabic. Calvin takes the other side of the opening question, since a question makes a thing stronger, the asker showing what he asks is too plain to be denied, so that Ephraim was unworthy of honour and no object of delight, having annihilated the favour of his adoption so far as he could; he explains why the waymarks were needed, since men carried into Chaldea assumed the way back closed and lived among foreigners as though dead to the land, knowing they had forfeited it and not believing the punishment temporary; and he gives the verb of the reproach its literal force of going round, calling circuits the crooked speculations the unbelieving weary themselves with.

Clarke has heaps of stones such as men set up in the desert to find the way back, and puts it bluntly: mark the road to Babylon, for thither you shall go and from it as certainly return. On the disputed clause he is equally sure no such meaning as the Incarnation is in the words or context, mentions an emendation in two manuscripts giving the wife shall return to her husband, doubts that would be called a new thing, and prefers a weak people overcoming the strong man who had oppressed them. Wesley keeps the received reading of the clause about speaking, drawing from it that since the threatenings God has remembered him with a father's compassion, agrees they must mind the way their captors take, and reads the last clause of the church, small in numbers against many and powerful enemies, prevailing all the same.

Henry holds the position the other two are refusing: the new and extraordinary thing is a creation, a work of almighty power, the human nature of Christ formed by the Holy Ghost, set here to encourage the exiles home.

debates.question: Does the question Is Ephraim my dear son expect yes or no?

positions.position: Yes; the negative form usually denies more vehemently, but that runs against the scope of the passage.
Yes, and far the better reading, since every word of reproof or invitation here carries a loving remembrance.
No; the question makes the thing stronger, and Ephraim was unworthy of honour and no object of delight.

debates.question: What does it mean that a woman shall compass a man?

positions.position: An inversion of courtship: the erring wife shall woo her divine husband, and the Incarnation reading belongs to dreams rather than realities.
A weak and defenceless people overcoming the strong man who oppressed them; no Incarnation meaning is in the words or the context.
The human nature of Christ, a creation and a work of almighty power, promised as encouragement to the exiles.
The church, small in numbers against many and powerful enemies, prevailing all the same.

outliers.claim: Settles the sense the English translators intended by quoting a line of Shakespeare in which to compass a woman is to woo and win her.
Explains the need for waymarks psychologically: men carried off assumed the road back was closed and lived among foreigners as though dead to their own land, believing the forfeit permanent.

themes: Is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child? for since I spake against him, I do earnestly remember him still: therefore my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him, saith the Lord.
Set thee up waymarks, make thee high heaps: set thine heart toward the highway, even the way which thou wentest: turn again, O virgin of Israel, turn again to these thy cities.
How long wilt thou go about, O thou backsliding daughter? for the Lord hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man.

23.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; As yet they shall use this speech in the land of Judah and in the cities thereof, when I shall bring again their captivity; The Lord bless thee, O habitation of justice, and mountain of holiness. And there shall dwell in Judah itself, and in all the cities thereof together, husbandmen, and they that go forth with flocks. For I have satiated the weary soul, and I have replenished every sorrowful soul. Upon this I awaked, and beheld; and my sleep was sweet unto me. Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man, and with the seed of beast. And it shall come to pass, that like as I have watched over them, to pluck up, and to break down, and to throw down, and to destroy, and to afflict; so will I watch over them, to build, and to plant, saith the Lord. In those days they shall say no more, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge. But every one shall die for his own iniquity: every man that eateth the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch report expositors who refer the waking to God, since God speaks in the context and the psalms sometimes call on him to awake, and answer that a man may say his sleep was sweet but God may not; on the sour grape they reject the reading which makes the fathers begin eating before the children's teeth were blunted, since the tenses set the blunting down as a result of the eating, so the saying means children atone for their fathers' misdeeds. Ellicott turns the eye from the northern kingdom to Judah, which shares the restoration, once more a faithful city with righteousness in it, the holy mountain naming the Temple hill; on the husbandmen and shepherds he draws an ideal of a people pastoral without being nomadic and agricultural yet sharing the culture and safety of cities, in sharp contrast to the ruined fields round the prophet; he hears in the satisfying of the weary an anticipation of the thought and almost the language of the Gospel; he lists two readings of the waking, one making it the husband who dreamt of his wife's return and another a psalm quotation about freedom from dark dreams, and finds the prophet's own words far more natural; and he makes the next promise turn on the prophet's own call some twenty-three years earlier, the almond, the wakeful or watching tree, with the play on its name, and the verbs of his commission all returning, but the work that was mostly rooting out and pulling down now the happier one of building and planting.

Gill agrees with Clarke that the oracle had been delivered in a dream from which the prophet woke at the last words, keeps the weariness of the satisfied soul and applies it to sinners at their first awakening, labouring after a righteousness they cannot find till they come to Christ, noting that the verb means not to satisfy only but to inebriate; on the proverb he takes it forward, that after the captivity no public calamity would fall for the fathers' sins and their own together, but for their own alone. Calvin disputes the rendering of the satisfied soul, since the word is commonly given as weary but he takes it for thirsty, citing a psalm where a soul is like dry land, weariness not being properly said of land, and noting the paired verb means to water or satiate; he explains the waking from the opposite feeling, since considering these terrible judgments the prophet had been as though overwhelmed with sleep, in which, as in darkness, men cannot tell black from white; he supplies the objection answered by the promise of watching, that a God who allowed the ruin might have prevented it, and replies that the hand which chastised can relieve whenever it pleases; and he notes another prophet quotes the same complaint about sour grapes, and finds a pagan poet telling his countrymen that the Roman undeservedly pays for his fathers' faults, adding that the proverb will die out because men tamed by their evils will see at last that God had not dealt severely without cause.

Clarke agrees the oracle was delivered in a dream, and passes on another suggestion, that the words are a wish, a prophet who cannot live to see such days asking to wake from his tomb, content to go back once he had; on the proverb he gives the same sense and correction as Keil and Delitzsch, that no child suffers divine punishment for a father's sin except so far as he acts the same way himself. Wesley notes the two divine titles prefacing these promises, one asserting power to do the thing and the other the goodness that means it.
Henry has the prophet going back to sleep on purpose, hoping for more, and not disappointed.

debates.question: Whose sleep was sweet?

positions.position: The prophet's, the oracle having been delivered in a dream from which he woke.
The prophet's, since a man may say his sleep was sweet but God may not, whatever expositors have made of the divine speaker.
The prophet's, far more naturally than the husband dreaming of his wife's return or a psalm quotation about freedom from dark dreams.
The prophet's, the sleep being the stupor into which the sight of these judgments had thrown him.

debates.question: Is the satisfied soul weary or thirsty?

positions.position: Thirsty; weariness cannot properly be said of the dry land the psalm compares it to, and the paired verb means to water.
Weary, and the verb means not merely to satisfy but to inebriate.
Both hunger and weariness, in an anticipation of the language of the Gospel.

outliers.claim: Dates the promise about watching to the prophet's own call some twenty-three years earlier, and finds the almond, the wakeful tree, and the verbs of his commission all returning, with the destroying work now turned to building and planting.
Passes on a reading of the waking as a wish, in which a prophet who cannot live to see such days asks to be allowed to wake from his tomb, and would go back content once he had seen them.

themes: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; As yet they shall use this speech in the land of Judah and in the cities thereof, when I shall bring again their captivity; The Lord bless thee, O habitation of justice, and mountain of holiness.
And there shall dwell in Judah itself, and in all the cities thereof together, husbandmen, and they that go forth with flocks.
For I have satiated the weary soul, and I have replenished every sorrowful soul.
Upon this I awaked, and beheld; and my sleep was sweet unto me.
Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man, and with the seed of beast.

And it shall come to pass, that like as I have watched over them, to pluck up, and to break down, and to throw down, and to destroy, and to afflict; so will I watch over them, to build, and to plant, saith the Lord.
In those days they shall say no more, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.
But every one shall die for his own iniquity: every man that eateth the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge.

31.pericope_label: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the Lord: But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the Lord, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch define the term, since to cut a covenant is not to make an appointment but to establish mutual obligations, God bestowing his favours and men bound to the commands laid on them; they refuse to fix the day of the taking by the hand either to the departure from Egypt or the ceremony at Sinai, referring it to the whole exodus, which ended only at the entry into the land; and they set the phrase for putting the law within them against the standing expression for setting it before them, and writing on the heart against writing on tables of stone. Ellicott asks his readers to feel how bold the announcement is, since familiarity hides it, but a covenant delivered with every conceivable sanction as from God is here set aside as a man repeals an earthly law, and whoever could say that without trembling must have been sure he was himself taught of God and that the new teaching stood higher; he traces what came of the phrase, the words used at the last supper, the argument of the letter to the Hebrews, the doctrine of justification by faith, and the titles by which the two collections of Scripture are still known; and he says the experiment of a law requiring righteousness had been tried and failed, so what remained was the hope, now turned into assurance, of a power imparting righteousness, written in the inward parts where God requires truth.

Gill locates the newness in the older covenant's defects: it was not properly one of works but typical, faulty in some sense or at least kept by faulty persons, and made with Israelites only, where this belongs to Jews and Gentiles alike. Calvin makes the passage turn on a comparison, since the promise is not of the dignity they had lost but of something better, and as the law was a rule of the most perfect doctrine nothing superior could be hoped for without Christ; take Christ away and we must remain in the law. He keeps the contrast sharp because no Jew thought God could add anything better to the law, and those who valued it least were loudest that heaven and earth would sooner mix than any change be made in it, while they clung to what God had instituted only for a time. He then raises the obvious objection against himself, whether the grace of regeneration was wanting to the fathers under the law, calls the suggestion preposterous, and answers that those regenerated then obtained the favour through Christ, so that it was transferred to them from another source, the power of penetrating the heart never having been inherent in the law but lent to it by the Gospel; what he concedes is that the grace was rare and little known then and has been poured out more abundantly since.

Clarke fixes the time as the sealing of vision and prophecy, the assuming of the body prepared, the laying down of the life and the ascension by which the Spirit's gift was obtained. Wesley denies the covenant is new in substance, since it was made with Abraham and with the people afterwards; it is new in being revealed after a new manner, more fully and plainly, in excluding the ceremonial law, and in the far greater efficacy of the Spirit attending it. He states the distinction between the covenants flatly, that the first shows duty and the second brings the grace of regeneration by which the heart is changed and enabled for duty; and he reaches Calvin's answer in his own words, that all under the law who came to salvation were saved by this new covenant, but it was not then evidently exhibited and regenerating grace was not so common as it has since become.

debates.question: In what sense is the covenant new?

positions.position: Not in substance, since it was made with Abraham; new in its manner of revelation, in excluding the ceremonial law, and in the greater efficacy of the Spirit.
New in that the older covenant was typical and faulty, or kept by faulty persons, and made with Israelites only where this reaches Gentiles too.
New in offering something better than the dignity lost, which without Christ could not be hoped for at all, since the law was already a rule of perfect doctrine.
New in writing the law within instead of setting it before them, on the heart instead of tables of stone.

debates.question: Was the grace of regeneration wanting to the fathers under the law?

positions.position: No; those regenerated then obtained the favour through Christ, the power of penetrating the heart being lent to the law by the Gospel, though the grace was rare and little known.
No; all under the law who came to salvation were saved by this new covenant, though it was not then evidently exhibited.

outliers.claim: Asks his readers to feel the boldness of a prophet setting aside a covenant delivered with every conceivable divine sanction, as a man repeals an earthly law, and to consider what confidence that took.
Observes that those who valued the law least were loudest in insisting heaven and earth would sooner mix than any change be made in it, while clinging to what God had instituted only for a time.

themes: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:

Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the Lord:

But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the Lord, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.

34.pericope_label: And they shall teach no more every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the Lord: for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them, saith the Lord: for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the verse out of a mood rather than a doctrine, since behind it lies the profound sense of failure that oppressed this prophet as it has oppressed many true teachers since: what had come of all the machinery of ritual and instruction the law had provided so abundantly, the repeated exhortations to know the Lord having become a dreary monotony like an old worm-eaten homily? To know him as he is would take nothing less than a revelation of his presence to each man's own heart, and that is what is promised here to whoever will receive it. On the last clause he is careful: the promise to remember sin no more repeats the promise to forgive but does it after the manner of men, since our thought of God as knowing everything rules out any limit on his knowledge such as forgetting would imply; what is meant is that he will be to the man who repents as men are to men when they forget and forgive, treating past offences as though they had never happened so far as they touch the soul's communion with him, however their consequences run on.

Gill defends the ministry, since the words cannot mean the outward preaching of the word, which will be needless only in the New Jerusalem and is needed in every period before it, nor do they forbid brotherly instruction or Christian conversation; what they exclude is the private man's pretended revelation and the magisterial dictate of a man in office, the written word being the only rule, or else the saying is comparative and not absolute. Calvin says fanatics have ignorantly abused the passage to put down teaching altogether, and answers that the words are hyperbole in the service of a comparison: it is not said that no man shall teach his neighbour, but that no man shall need to say know the Lord, and that phrase names the first elements of the faith, so the promise is that God's people will no longer be alphabetarians kept in the rudiments as the ancient people were, the least of the faithful now seeing more clearly what belongs to salvation than the most learned did then. He then sets the verse against another prophet who has each man taking his neighbour by the hand to go up and be taught, reconciling them by saying one denies that the people will still need first principles while the other has them helping each other on; and he cautions that the knowledge is not said to be equal in all, experience proving otherwise and the measure of God's gifts being according to his own pleasure.

Clarke turns the promise into a report on his own century: it is to be a time of universal light, when all shall know God from the least to the greatest and children shall be taught to read the new covenant and understand the terms of their salvation, and a time of general pardon, with multitudes daily receiving the witness of the Spirit and confessing it in their lives. He then names what he takes for the fulfilment, the age of Bibles, of Sunday schools and of village preaching. Wesley puts the last clause at the root of everything else in the passage, making the free pardon and remission of sins the thing all the rest of this grace grows from.

debates.question: Does the promise abolish teaching?

positions.position: No; it excludes the private man's pretended revelation and the magisterial dictate of an officeholder, not preaching or brotherly instruction, and may in any case be comparative.
No; it is hyperbole, and what will be needless is the elementary summons to know the Lord, not teaching itself.
It promises universal light, which the age of Bibles, Sunday schools and village preaching is already realising.

debates.question: What does it mean that God will remember their sin no more?

positions.position: It is said after the manner of men, since God's knowledge has no limits; he will treat past offences as though they had never happened, so far as they touch communion with him.
It is the root the rest of the grace grows from, the free pardon and remission of sins.

outliers.claim: Names the fulfilment of the promise in his own lifetime, in what he calls the age of Bibles, of Sunday schools and of village preaching.

Reconciles this verse with another prophet's picture of neighbours taking each other by the hand to be taught, by saying one denies the need of first principles while the other has men helping each other on beyond them.

themes: And they shall teach no more every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the Lord: for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them, saith the Lord: for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.

35.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord, which giveth the sun for a light by day, and the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night, which divideth the sea when the waves thereof roar; The Lord of hosts is his name: If those ordinances depart from before me, saith the Lord, then the seed of Israel also shall cease from being a nation before me for ever. Thus saith the Lord; If heaven above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth searched out beneath, I will also cast off all the seed of Israel for all that they have done, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the thought of the previous verse returns with a modification, since besides the stability of nature standing as a parable of the steadfastness of God's purposes there is now implied a sense that a finite mind can no more fathom how he works those purposes out than it can measure what to the prophet was an illimitable heaven and an unsearchable earth.

Gill keeps to the plain sense of the ordinances, that the lights should leave their proper course, fail of their functions, desert their master or disobey his orders, and takes the measuring literally enough to name what could not be measured, either the distance between the highest heavens and the earth or the extent of the heavens from one end to the other. Calvin explains why so much weight had to be put on the argument, since it was hard to believe a people would not merely recover what they had lost but be made happier than before, when the church was in complete despondency, and even a church raised a hundred times from the dead might be crushed a hundred times again with grievous evils still ahead. On the description of the heavens he observes that the prophets spoke popularly and according to common notions, so that God is made to speak of the daily circuit of the sun and moon; had they philosophised as the astronomers do, and spoken of the monthly course of the moon and the yearly course of the sun, the common people could not have followed, and they were content to state what even children could take in. He reads the last comparison as the impossibility of God forgetting his covenant, since exile might have looked like a permanent death and made the truth of God come to nothing, and though a condition was attached the covenant never rested on the integrity of men, so that God is not a liar though every one of them proved faithless; setting impossible things before us is his way of making us know he will at last be reconciled to a people he has justly punished, and none of it could comfort a hypocrite.

Clarke turns the comparison into a claim about his own day, that as surely as the sun gives light by day so surely will this people continue distinct from every other, and holds the prophecy has been literally fulfilled so far, since every attempt in any country to naturalise them and merge them with its population has come to nothing; he names the most recent instance, an effort made in his own country in the year he was writing and supported, he says, by the strongest public interest, which had failed like the rest, and refers the failure to the purpose declared in these verses. Wesley defines the ordinances as the establishments by which God works natural causes in their order.

Henry treats these verses as the ratification of everything promised before: glorious things have been said, but may they be depended on? What is secured is that while the world stands God will have a church in it, which may be brought very low and will be raised again, and two things are offered to confirm it, the building of the world and the rebuilding of Jerusalem; he who built all things at first is the same who makes all things now, so the constancy of the kingdom of nature may encourage us to trust the promise for the continuance of the kingdom of grace.

debates.question: What is the force of the appeal to the ordinances of sun and moon?

positions.position: The constancy of the kingdom of nature is offered as security for the continuance of the kingdom of grace.
A guarantee that this people will remain distinct from every other, which he holds has been literally fulfilled down to his own day.
An assurance that God cannot forget his covenant, since it never rested on the integrity of men.
A parable of the steadfastness of God's purposes, joined to a sense that a finite mind cannot fathom how he works them out.

debates.question: Why does the passage describe the sun and moon as it does?

positions.position: Because the prophets spoke popularly, stating what even children could grasp rather than what the astronomers would say.
Because these are the establishments by which God works natural causes in their order.
Because the point is what would happen if the lights left their course, failed of their functions or disobeyed their master.

outliers.claim: States a principle of accommodation, that the prophets described the daily circuit of sun and moon because a monthly and yearly account, such as the astronomers give, would have been beyond the common people.
Cites an attempt made in his own country in the very year he was writing, backed by strong public interest, as a failed instance of what he says the verse forbids.

themes: Thus saith the Lord, which giveth the sun for a light by day, and the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night, which divideth the sea when the waves thereof roar; The Lord of hosts is his name:
If those ordinances depart from before me, saith the Lord, then the seed of Israel also shall cease from being a nation before me for ever.
Thus saith the Lord; If heaven above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth searched out beneath, I will also cast off all the seed of Israel for all that they have done, saith the Lord.

38.pericope_label: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that the city shall be built to the Lord from the tower of Hananeel unto the gate of the corner. And the measuring line shall yet go forth over against it upon the hill Gareb, and shall compass about to Goath. And the whole valley of the dead bodies, and of the ashes, and all the fields unto the brook of Kidron, unto the corner of the horse gate toward the east, shall be holy unto the Lord; it shall not be plucked up, nor thrown down any more for ever.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the valley for that of Hinnom, the word covering carcases of beasts and of men left unburied after a judgment, and connect the name with its pollution under Josiah. Ellicott admits the drop feels like an anti-climax, from the loftiest promises in the book to a list of obscure landmarks, but explains it by how vividly the restored city stood before the prophet's mind, as before an earlier prophet's and, on a far larger scale, a later one; he notes neither of the two hills named occurs elsewhere, so any position is guesswork, derives the first from the word for a leper, setting it outside the walls where such sufferers lived, and offers a northern hill named by the historian of the war, while calling the second of doubtful etymology and reporting a scholar who makes it high-towering, for the height above the Kidron later crowned by a fortress. He makes us look at the valley as the prophet did during the siege, filled with corpses lying in the streets, the ashes of burnt houses choking them with rubble, the open ground running to the Kidron, a scene of unspeakable desolation which he sees in vision cleansed and as holy as the Temple precincts.

Gill reports a rabbi saying the prophecy belongs to a later redemption and was never fulfilled under the second temple, and takes the rebuilding himself as a figure of the church, holiness and perpetuity being ascribed to it; he also stops at a word read but not written, the vowel points standing where letters do not, and makes an argument of it, that those who deny the antiquity of the pointing should consider it, the Jews never having suffered anything added to their Bible. Calvin keeps the historical city and holds the point is that its extent and splendour after the return would not fall short of what they were under David, comparing a later prophet making the same promise to a people whose restored city at first fell far short of the old; he reports that most interpreters take the measuring line going forth to mean enlargement beyond the old walls and declines it, since the other prophet promises the city shall be inhabited in its own place, so the comparison is between ancient greatness and greatness to come; he declines the place-names outright, saying he can tell us little because the ancient situation of the city is unknown and those who conjecture about such things only display their ignorance; and he takes the ashes for those swept from the altar after the sacrifices were burnt, saying the other name was given because a host of enemies had been destroyed there in Hezekiah's day, so the mercy might stay known to later generations.

Clarke says the city meant cannot be the one rebuilt after Babylon, for two reasons, that this one is much greater in extent and permanent, never to be thrown down, so if the words are literal at all they mean a city built at some later ingathering; he notes the two hills named lay outside the old limits and are destined to fall within the new, and identifies the second name with Golgotha, the heap of Gotha, which as the place of the crucifixion lay outside the city; he ends with a Latin line bidding the happy times make speed. Wesley takes the measuring line to mean the city will be built round about on its old foundations, gives the same derivations of the valley names as Calvin, and reads the perpetuity of the promise as belonging to the church, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail.

debates.question: Which city is promised here?

positions.position: Not the one rebuilt after Babylon, since this is greater in extent and permanent; a city of some later ingathering, if the words are literal at all.
The church, under the figure of a rebuilt Jerusalem, since holiness and perpetuity are both ascribed to it.
The historical city, whose extent and splendour after the return would not fall short of what they were under David.

debates.question: Is the new city larger than the old, or the same?

positions.position: Larger, since the hills named lay outside the old limits and are to fall within the new.
The same footprint, built round about on its old foundations.
The same place; most interpreters read enlargement out of the measuring line, but another prophet promises the city shall be inhabited where it stood.

outliers.claim: Uses a word that is read but not written, with the vowel points standing where the consonants do not, as an argument for the antiquity of the Hebrew pointing.
Refuses the place-names entirely, saying the ancient situation of the city is unknown and that those who conjecture about such things only display their own ignorance.

themes: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that the city shall be built to the Lord from the tower of Hananeel unto the gate of the corner.
And the measuring line shall yet go forth over against it upon the hill Gareb, and shall compass about to Goath.

And the whole valley of the dead bodies, and of the ashes, and all the fields unto the brook of Kidron, unto the corner of the horse gate toward the east, shall be holy unto the Lord; it shall not be plucked up, nor thrown down any more for ever.
